newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain honours foreign veterans of its Civil War.
newsitem.headline: Spain honours foreign veterans of its Civil War.

text.p: More than 100 veterans of the International Brigades began to arrive on Sunday to honour comrades-in-arms who died for the Republican cause in Spain's 1936-39 Civil War.
"Long live the Republic!" shouted 86-year-old Emanuel Mink, a Polish-born French citizen, as he arrived at the city's Barajas airport.

Mink was among the first of 400 veterans expected in Madrid this week, 60 years after foreign volunteers took up arms in the name of democracy in a conflict which became an ideological rehearsal for World War Two.

The Brigades were mainly recruited by communist parties and trade unions in Europe and North America, with support from the Soviet Union. The armies of Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy aided the rightwing or Loyalist side.
Republican defeat in 1939 left General Francisco Franco to rule Spain as a military dictator until his death in 1975.

But the story of the International Brigades is immortalised in books such as George Orwell's "Homage to Catalonia", published in 1938, and films like British director Ken Loach's recent "Land and Freedom".
More than 40,000 volunteered. A third fell in battle. Of those still alive, many are too old or too ill to travel.

Organisers said veterans from more than 30 countries would attend memorial events including a reception in Spain's parliament on November 6 which Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar is expected to attend.
But the ceremony could leave a bitter taste in their mouths after a decision by the previous Socialist government to offer former brigade members honourary Spanish citizenship fell flat.
The Spanish parliament last November voted unanimously in favour of the measure, fulfilling a promise made by Spanish Prime Minister Juan Negrin almost 60 years ago.

Brigade veterans who had waited all their lives for the honour began to apply for Spanish passports, but discovered that in order to accept them, they would have to renounce their citizenship and all the health and pension benefits available to them at home.
"It's like a cruel joke," said an article in daily El Pais. "When parliament unanimously approved the proposal, nobody thought the decision would run into these prosaic difficulties."
Efforts to find a solution have so far met with no response from the conservative government.
Despite the disappointment, brigade veterans are likely to focus on emotional reunions with old comrades and ceremonies honouring the dead.

These included men and women, poets and miners, young and old who banded together in what poet Louis MacNeice described as a "rag bag army" against fascism, united by the Republican battle cry of "No pasaran!" ("They shall not pass!").
Emanuel Mink, who hadn't returned to Spain since the Civil war, said he looked forward to meeting up with old friends.
He brought with him a manuscript of his memoirs and a photograph of his meeting with Communist heroine Dolores Ibarruri, known as La Pasionaria.
"I'm still the same person I was then," he said.
